analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare run its own drug plan and negotiate prices directly with drugmakers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote, ending when the 111th Congress expired in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a government-run Medicare prescription drug plan offered nationwide alongside the private plans in Medicare Part D. It directed the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate prices directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers, waiving the part of the 2003 Medicare law that bars Medicare from negotiating drug prices. The government plan would have used a list of covered drugs favoring lower-cost, clinically effective options, and beneficiaries denied a drug would have gotten a formal appeals process.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries with drug coverage. They would have gained a new plan option run by Medicare itself, with prices negotiated by the government and premiums set nationally rather than varying by private plan, plus a clear appeals process if a needed drug was not covered [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate drug purchase prices with pharmaceutical manufacturers for a Medicare-run plan, expressly overriding the existing prohibition on Medicare negotiating drug prices [S3].

Requires the Secretary to offer at least one Medicare-operated drug plan with a service area covering the entire United States, available every year beginning in 2010, alongside the private Part D plans [S3].

Sets a single national monthly premium based on the plan's average per-person cost, and requires the plan's drug list to favor drugs that cost less and work as well or better, using tools like tiered copays and generic substitution [S3].

Creates a defined appeals process for denials under the Medicare plan, including an initial review by the Secretary and an outside independent review, aimed at getting medically necessary non-formulary drugs to patients quickly [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear lower negotiated prices, and the private insurers that sell Medicare Part D plans would face a direct government-run competitor for enrollees [S3]. Taxpayers would fund the plan's administrative operation through Medicare [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug manufacturers and private drug-plan insurers

drawbacks.text: The plan's formulary tools explicitly include prior authorization, step therapy, and reference pricing, meaning some beneficiaries could face delays or be required to try cheaper drugs first before getting the drug their doctor prescribed [S3].
The bill would have eliminated federal fallback prescription drug plans after 2009, narrowing one existing option as the new government plan replaced it [S3].

Critics of government drug negotiation have long argued that strong price bargaining paired with a restrictive formulary can limit access to newer drugs, and the bill's own design relies on excluding drugs that cost more without proven added clinical benefit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For beneficiaries the upside was concrete: a public option in drug coverage with government-negotiated prices and a national premium, in a program where the 2003 law deliberately bars Medicare from negotiating. The tradeoff is real but narrower — the plan would use managed-care tools like step therapy and prior authorization, so some patients might have had to jump through hoops for certain drugs, though an appeals process was written in to limit that. On balance the bill was designed to transfer savings from drug prices to beneficiaries.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2009 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill with four Senate colleagues on January 27, 2009 [S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action was ever taken — the committee held no markup, the Senate never debated it, and no vote of any kind occurred [S5].
The bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and the private insurers that sell Medicare Part D plans, who kept the status quo: Medicare still barred from negotiating drug prices and no government-run plan competing for their customers.

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois and lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 27, 2009 and spoke for it on the Senate floor at introduction [S5].

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: The Senate's sole Independent, Senator from Vermont

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill, leaving it to die at referral — during the same period his committee wrote the health care overhaul without including government drug-price negotiation.

against.name: PhRMA and the pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed Medicare drug-price negotiation during the 2009 health care debate and spent heavily on lobbying and advertising that year to keep negotiation out of the final legislation.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or the chamber's one Independent, and no vote ever occurred to test broader support; the bill's fate was decided in a committee run by a Democratic chair with no recorded positions from the full Senate.

industries.note: The bill would have required HHS to negotiate purchase prices for drugs sold under the new Medicare plan, ending the industry's sole-seller pricing in Part D. Beneficiaries' savings under the bill come directly out of the prices drugmakers charge.

industries.industry: Private Medicare Part D insurers and drug-plan sponsors
industries.note: A national government-run drug plan would have competed directly with private plans for enrollees, with premiums set by the government. The industry's revenue from Medicare drug coverage is the reason the status quo persists in its current form.
